rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: Passengers should keep seat belts fastened throughout flight and must fasten them when the seat-belt sign is illuminated.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: During turbulence, passengers should remain seated and follow crew instructions.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: Safety briefings and aircraft-specific safety cards identify exits, restraints and emergency equipment.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: Cabin baggage should be stowed securely so it does not create an additional hazard during unexpected movement.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: Aviation organisations must report qualifying safety occurrences through the Mandatory Occurrence Reporting system.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: Occurrence reports help identify trends and support corrective action before risks lead to more serious outcomes.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: Employees should use appropriate internal or regulatory reporting channels when an incident or safety concern occurs.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: A just-culture reporting environment supports learning while preserving legal reporting obligations.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: Turbulence risk depends on weather, aircraft, route, altitude, warning time, restraint use, cabin activity and crew response.

rows.source: CAA cabin turbulence and occurrence-reporting safety
rows.verified: CAA cabin evidence is flight-, aircraft-, passenger-, weather-, reporting- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: Train-protection systems reduce risks from signals passed at danger and movements exceeding safe speed limits.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: Train protection can automatically apply brakes when a train passes its movement authority or approaches a hazard too quickly.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: Railway Safety Regulations require an in-service train-protection system for applicable train and infrastructure operations.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: TPWS provides a minimum intervention capability, while ATP systems provide a higher level of protection where reasonably practicable.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: ETCS and communications-based train control are forms of automatic train protection.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: Operators and infrastructure managers should plan upgrades and manage migration toward higher levels of protection.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: ROGS requires effective safety-management systems, cooperation and competent safety-critical workers.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: ORR identifies overspeeding as a significant precursor to derailment or collision requiring coordinated controls, data, training and investigation.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: Train-protection risk depends on signalling, speed profile, equipment fitment, system availability, driver response, infrastructure and operating context.

rows.source: ORR train-protection and overspeeding controls
rows.verified: ORR train-protection evidence is route-, system-, train-, operator-, event- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level collision probability.
